function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents you’ll need to add to the repo.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to your GitHub account from here, but the commands below will do it for you locally.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image (you can change the version if you prefer)
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-slim` is a lightweight base image that contains Node.js.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` installs only production dependencies, keeping the image small.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** (the default for many Node.js examples).  
> * Adjust the `CMD` line if your entry point is different (e.g., `index.js`).

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` in the repo root with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of your Node.js app.  
> * Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80.  
> * Replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image you’ll push (see the GitHub Actions section).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a directory `.github/workflows` if it doesn’t exist, then add a file named `ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI – Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Optional: Deploy to a Kubernetes cluster (requires kubeconfig in secrets)
      # Uncomment the following block if you want automatic deployment
      #
      # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      #   with:
      #     manifests: k8s-deployment.yaml
      #     kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **What you need to set up**  
> * The workflow uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> * The image will be pushed to `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
> * If you want to deploy automatically, add a `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` secret containing your kubeconfig (base64‑encoded) and uncomment the deployment step.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, build the Docker image, and push it to GHCR.  
> If you enabled the optional deployment step, it will also apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Verify the Docker image**  
   ```bash
   docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
   docker run -p 3000:3000 ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
   ```
   Open `http://localhost:3000` to see your app.

2. **Apply the Kubernetes manifests** (if you have a cluster configured)  
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
   ```

---

That’s it! 🎉  
If you hit any snags (e.g., the app listens on a different port, or you’re using a different registry), just tweak the files accordingly. Happy coding!
